newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels seize Permet, vow to hold south.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels seize Permet, vow to hold south.

text.p: Albanian rebels seized the southern town of Permet, extending their hold towards the east, and vowed not to surrender their weapons until Albanian President Sali Berisha resigned.

Five people were killed and six injured in Sunday's fighting that put this important southern town under the rebels' control hours before Berisha struck a deal with opposition parties to hold early elections.

"A group of soldiers left yesterday and as they were leaving they started shooting at people in the main square. There were many dead and injured. People took guns from the police station and two barracks and we shot back," eyewitness Hecuran Bejollari told Reuters.
One of the injured was in critical condition and all had been wounded by bullets, doctor Lefteri Kiriako of Permet hospital told Reuters.
Most of the town's 12,000 residents gathered at the main square on Monday and were listening to announcements from speakers urging them to remain calm and not to fire their guns aimlessly in the air.

"We will try to find a way to calm people. A rebel council that has been elected will distribute food, gas and other necessities," said mayor Spartak Kondi. "We will return our weapons when Berisha resigns."
Most public buildings were sprayed with bullets and the town's police station was still on fire.
Journalists driving from the rebel-held town of Gjirokaster found no roadblocks on the way to Permet, which is on the main highway southeast from rebel-held Tepelene.
A military base near Permet was used for staging a failed army raid on Gjirokaster last week. The town's two army barracks were looted by rebels but it was unclear how many weapons were taken.
"On Saturday Berisha sent 2,000 soldiers. They have now left towards Erseke and Korce," said army captain Vladimir Culi, who has joined the insurgents.
He said about 16 villages nearby, including Kelcyre, had been captured by rebels.
The insurgents have turned a cold shoulder to Berisha's offer of amnesty if they turned in their weapons and his promise of early elections.
Berisha, facing a growing armed revolt in the south, agreed with all political parties to hold a new general election in June -- three years ahead of schedule.
But the rebels in the south said they wanted Berisha himself to resign before surrendering thousands of weapons -- including tanks and heavy artillery -- which have been looted from state arsenals.
Berisha is accused by the rebels of standing by while five fraudulent pyramid investment schemes collapsed in January, wiping out the savings of thousands of Albanians.
The armed revolt began in the Adriatic coastal town of Vlore and spread throughout the southwest corner of the country.

Rebel leaders, many former army officers, were in contact on Monday in the main towns of Gjirokaster, Vlore, Sarande and Delvine to discuss Berisha's deal with the opposition. They said they would discuss the agreement with opposition leaders in Tirana as well.
